story: The Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world. Water in the bay rocks back and forth with a natural period of about 13 hours, and the Atlantic tide, arriving every 12 hours and 25 minutes, pushes it in step, like a well-timed push on a swing; the narrowing, shallowing bay forces the water higher still. At the park the range reaches 12 metres, and at low tide you can walk more than a kilometre across the flats from Alma Beach to the water's edge. Each day the tides come about an hour later, following the lunar day of 24 hours and 52 minutes.

Most of the park is not coast but the Caledonia Highlands, rounded hills of the Appalachians that rise 300 metres from the shore. During the last ice age they carried their own ice caps, and when the ice melted about 13,000 years ago it left sand and gravel over the land and in the valleys, which rivers such as the Upper Salmon and Point Wolfe have been carrying to the sea ever since. The forest is Acadian, in the transition between the conifers of the boreal north and the hardwoods to the south, and black bear, moose, deer and coyote live in it. More than 25 waterfalls drop through the valleys.

The Mi'gmaq, Wolastoqiyik and Peskotomuhkati have lived in this part of New Brunswick since time immemorial; the park lies on unceded Mi'gmaq territory, and inland portages linked the Saint John and Petitcodiac river systems on either side of it. European settlement came late, around 1825, when immigrants from Scotland, Ireland and England took land grants. The thin, acidic soils were poor for farming but good for trees, and sawmills, shipbuilding and fishing supplied Saint John and markets abroad. Point Wolfe, with its sawmill at the river mouth, became the main village, but by 1922 the large mills, river drives and shipbuilding had gone and many families had moved away.

The logging had clogged rivers with sawmill waste and kept Atlantic salmon from their spawning grounds. In 1948 the area near Alma was chosen as New Brunswick's first national park, both to protect it and to bring work to the region; it was proclaimed on 10 April 1948 and opened on 29 July 1950. Since the early 2000s Parks Canada, Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Fort Folly First Nation have kept the endangered inner Bay of Fundy salmon alive in a live gene bank, and the park now raises wild smolts at sea to release as adults into its rivers. The park is the core of the Fundy Biosphere Reserve and a Dark-Sky Preserve.
howItWorks: Fundy is open all year and admission is charged at the entrance kiosks. As listed in November 2026, daily admission is $10.00 for an adult, and youth aged 17 and under get in free at every Parks Canada place. A Parks Canada Discovery Pass, $83.50 for an adult, $71.50 for a senior or $167.50 for a family or group of up to seven people arriving in one vehicle, covers admission at more than 80 Parks Canada places for 12 months; seasonal and Discovery passes and fishing permits are sold in the park. Under the Canada Strong Pass admission was free from 19 June to 7 September 2026; regular fees resumed on 8 September 2026.

The five frontcountry campgrounds, Headquarters, Chignecto North, Point Wolfe, Lakeview and Cannontown, together with the oTENTiks, yurts, Ôasis units, rustic cabins and the eight backcountry sites, are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service at reservation.pc.gc.ca or 1-877-737-3783. Bookings for the 2027 season open on Friday 5 February 2027 at 8 am Atlantic time. Backcountry campers must register with park staff at a visitor centre before setting out, camp only at the site on their permit, and drop the permit off, or phone the park, when they leave.

Fishing needs a national park fishing permit; provincial licences do not apply. Motors, gas or electric, are not allowed on any lake or river in the park, and off-road vehicles are banned. Recreational drones are prohibited, with fines of up to $25,000. Fires are allowed only in the metal fire boxes provided, using park firewood, and bringing in firewood from outside is prohibited. Pets must be on a leash and are not allowed at Bennett Lake beach, the swimming pool or the golf course.

sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-dickson-falls: The park's most popular trail: a 1.5-kilometre loop of boardwalk and stairs down a fern-filled ravine to its most photographed waterfall.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-third-vault-falls: The park's highest waterfall, 16 metres, at the end of a 3.7-kilometre trail downhill through mixed forest. Allow three to four hours return.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-laverty-falls: A curtain waterfall with a swimming hole below, 2.5 kilometres along a moderate trail.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-alma-beach: Next to Alma village and the Headquarters area: at low tide the flats run out more than a kilometre to the water's edge.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-point-wolfe-covered-bridge: The only covered bridge in a Canadian national park, at the site of the old sawmill village. Closed for repairs from 8 September to December 2026.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-herring-cove: A beach reached by stairs, one of the places Parks Canada recommends for watching the tide come in and go out.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-matthews-head: A 4.5-kilometre loop to a headland with wide coastal views and a sea stack.
sightNotes.poi-ca-fundy-caribou-plain: A 2.1-kilometre loop past beaver ponds to a raised bog with carnivorous plants.

chronology.text: European settlement begins in what is now the park, with immigrants from Scotland, Ireland and England.
By this year the large sawmills, river drives and shipbuilding have ended.
Fundy National Park, New Brunswick's first, is proclaimed in the Canada Gazette on 10 April.
The park is officially opened on 29 July; the Headquarters visitor centre dates from the same year.
Parks Canada, Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Fort Folly First Nation start a live gene bank for inner Bay of Fundy Atlantic salmon.
An advisory committee of Parks Canada and Mi'gmaq leadership is set up for the parks in New Brunswick.
Point Wolfe Covered Bridge closes from 8 September for repairs to extend its life.

safety: The tide here rises 9 to 12 metres. Check the tide times before walking on the sea floor, and keep an eye on the water so you are not cut off.
Several trails ford rivers. Crossings are closed with signs at the trailhead when the water is high; if you are unsure, do not cross.
Lakes and rivers have no lifeguards. Do not swim in strong current or dive into rivers; the Forty-Five River bridge pools are closed to swimming.
Black bears, moose, deer and coyotes live in the park. Keep your distance, never feed them, and store food in your vehicle or an animal-proof container.
Blacklegged ticks that can carry Lyme disease are active from April to November; check yourself after walking.
regulations: Do not feed or disturb wildlife, and do not collect plants, mushrooms, berries, antlers, rocks, driftwood or any other natural or historic object.
Fires only in the metal fire boxes, with park firewood; bringing firewood into the park is prohibited.
No motors on lakes or rivers, no off-road vehicles, and no recreational drones.
Camp only in designated sites; sleeping in vehicles at pullouts, trailheads and day-use areas is not allowed.
Pets on a leash at all times, and not at Bennett Lake beach, the pool or the golf course.

weather: The park lies across two climates. The coast has the cool summers and mild winters of the Bay of Fundy, with less snow, while the highlands inland have warmer summers and colder, snowier winters, and the difference is often plain on the same day: when the interior averages 22 °C in summer, the coast can be 6 °C cooler. Summer is the main season for camping and the tidal flats, and the hardwoods colour in autumn. In winter the park stays open for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, fat biking and tobogganing, with yurts and oTENTiks at Headquarters. Blacklegged ticks are active from April to November.
directions: Fundy is on Route 114 beside the village of Alma on New Brunswick's south-east coast, about an hour's drive from Moncton, an hour and a half from Saint John and two hours from Fredericton. From Saint John or Fredericton take Highway 1 towards Moncton and leave it at exit 211 for Route 114; from Moncton follow Route 114 south-west. There is no public transport to the park; the nearest bus terminals are in Sussex and Moncton, and the nearest airports are in Moncton, Saint John and Fredericton.
